Carpal fractures

Scaphoid fractures (75% of all carpal fractures)

Lunate

Triquetrum

Trapezium

Capitate

Hamate

Epidemiology

Scaphoid fractures account for 75% of all carpal fractures

Fractures of other carpal bones are all rare; they can be easily overlooked. Careful examination, X-rays inspection, especially after a significant traumatic mechanism, is important. If in still in doubt, CT or MRI are options.

A scaphoid fracture occur with a significant traumatic mechanisms, which would typically involve a sporting injury or high-energy fall. That is why it is more common in younger and active individuals.

Scaphoid fractures if missed, they can lead to morbidity as the risk of non-union can be high (14-50% if fracture is displaced)

If left untreated, arthritis, deformity and instability may develop within 5 years which leads to disability

Scaphoid fractures MOI

Scaphoid bone lies in the line of loading between the thumb and forearm

So it can fracture in case of axial loading on the wrist in forced flexion or extension and compression; e.g. fall on the outstretched hand

Scaphoid fractures

Fractures occur on three anatomical locations on the scaphoid:

Distal tubercule

Waist: 65% of all scaphoid fractures

Proximal pole

Scaphoid blood supply arises from the dorsal distal pole via a branch from the radial artery and the superficial palmar arch so proximal pole gets its blood supply by retrograde flow; so it is considered to have a poor blood supply and less likely to heal than distal pole (high risk of avascular necrosis)

Clinical features

Symptoms

Patient present with wrist pain and they report some type of injury mechanism like falling on the outstretched hand, or getting hit by some type of object

Physical examination

Look

In scaphoid fractures, the wrist appearance looks deceptively normal; but if you look closely, you notice fullness in the anatomical snuffbox

An isolated scaphoid fracture will not usually cause any deformity, but deformity may be seen when associated with a dislocation of the carpus: for example, trans-scaphoid peri lunate fracture-dislocation.

Feel

There is tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox and there is pain on axial loading on the thumb, and pain on pushing the scaphoid tubercle backwards (more specific for scaphoid fractures)

Physical examination

Move

In scaphoid fractures, there is limitation to wrist movements (more by pain than stiffness)

pain on passive ulnar deviation is highly specific to scaphoid fractures, conversely, lack of pain on ulnar deviation is highly indicative of absence of scaphoid fracture

Classification

Scaphoid fractures are classified according to the Herbert-Fischer classification (most commonly used classification)

Herbert classification is a 4 types classification system and it takes into consideration fracture stability and if it was acute/chronic

Herbert classification provides a guide to the management of scaphoid fractures

Herbert Type A and B are for acute scaphoid fractures while Type C and D for Chronic fractures

Herbert classification

  • Type A: acute stable fractures
  • Type A1: Tuberosity fracture
  • Type A2: Undisplaced Waist fracture
  • Type B: acute unstable fractures
  • Type B1: Oblique distal third fracture
  • Type B2: Displaced waist fracture
  • Type B3: Proximal third fractures
  • Type B4: Fracture dislocation
  • Type B5: Comminuted fracture
  • Type C: Chronic
  • Type C: Delayed union
  • Type D: Chronic
  • Type D1: Fibrous non-union
  • Type D2: Sclerotic non-union
  • Type B: acute unstable fractures
  • Type B1: Oblique distal third fracture
  • Type B2: Displaced waist fracture
  • Type B3: Proximal third fractures
  • Type B4: Fracture dislocation
  • Type B5: Comminuted fracture

Imaging

X-rays are the first line investigation modality for scaphoid fractures

Initially, four standard views are obtained:

PA with wrist in ulnar deviation (scaphoid view)

Lateral

Semi-pronated oblique

Semi-supinated oblique.

All must be carefully examined, often recent fracture only shows in the oblique views (other view are normal)

Look at the fracture line (transverse, or oblique)

Look at the location of the fracture line (waist, proximal pole or distal pole)

Look for displacement (translation, angulation or shortening)

If fracture line not visible, treat the clinical diagnosis and repeat x rays after 2 weeks (fracture line shows after a period of time due to bone resorption and movement)

15% of scaphoid fractures are not visible on initial x rays

MRI: highly sensitive for detecting scaphoid fractures and also very good in detecting soft tissue injuries such as scapholunate ligament injury; it is used initially if the x rays are normal and clinical examination highly suggest a fracture; but often not available in emergency departments

CT: This is also sensitive for detecting a fracture and is a suitable alternative to MRI. However, the risks associated with radiation must be considered and CT will not identify associated potentially significant soft tissue injuries around the carpus, such as a scapholunate ligament disruption.

Emergency treatment

Scaphoid Fractures are managed by: reduce-hold-exercise

There is no role for closed reduction in displaced scaphoid fractures

So emergency treatment is all about holding (immobilization) of the fracture in most cases by a below elbow backslab or a wrist splint and patient is reviewed again after a week in the fracture clinic for assessment and to determine definitive treatment

If a patient is suspected to have a fracture but the x rays are normal then patient is reviewed in the fracture clinic after 2 weeks to allow bone resorption and x rays is repeated (better fracture observation on x rays)

Definitive Treatment

Herbert type A1: tuberosity fractures

These are treated in a cast for 4-6 weeks

Non union is rare with these fractures => but if happens, it requires excision of a small fragment or grafting of larger fragment

Type A1: Tuberosity fracture

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

These are treated either by casting or by percutanous fixation

Casting: 90% of waist fractures heal in a neutral below elbow POP cast (thumb doesn’t have to be included in the cast) for 6-8 weeks

Type A2: Undisplaced Waist fracture

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

After that the cast is removed and wrist is examined clinically and radiologically by x rays, if wrist is painless and x rays is normal then treatment is complete; if still in doubt , CT scan is most reliable for confirming union

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

If tenderness on examination is present or fracture line still visible on x ray then cast reapplied for further 4 weeks

After 4 weeks, if wrist is painless and x ray is normal then cast is removed and treatment is complete, if tenderness is present or x rays showing signs of delayed healing (bone resporption and cavitation around the fracture) then bone grafting and internal fixation is indicated

Herbert type A2: Undisplaced waist fractures

Percutaneous fixation: it is considered in patients who want faster results (e.g. athletes) but impact and heavy load should still be avoided until fracture is fully healed

Percutaneous fixation is done by cannulated screws that are passed through mall incision in front of the scaphoid tubercle

Herbert type B fractures

Those also can be treated by casting but malunion and non union rates are higher

So it is better to reduce the fracture (closed if possible) and fix it with a compression screw => this will improve the union likelihood and reduce time of immobilization

Herbert Type C and D: Delayed union and non union

This is due to either poor blood supply or displacement of these fractures;

in delayed union fracture line becomes more apparent and hard border develops (making it seem like an extra carpal bone);

in non union cavitation appears on sides of the fracture

Type C: Delayed union

In distal pole and waist fracture non union, distal fragment rotate forward and proximal fragment rotate backwards giving an appearance of a round scaphoid tubercle (ring sign) on the PA view and dorsally tilted proximal pole and lunate on lateral view (DISI)

Non union of proximal pole doesn’t lead to malalignment but it does lead to avascular necrosis

Sometimes patient is seen for the first time after an old wrist sprain; x ray shows non united fracture with sclerosed edges maybe several years old, In older patients with low demands or those asymptomatic; non union maybe left untreated if patient agrees after discussion

3-4 weeks of casting may suffice to make patient comfortable once again and no further treatment is required

In the acute stage of a scaphoid fracture, by 3 months it maybe obvious if the fracture will unite or not; surgery should be advised especially in young patients because it would reduce the chance for osteoarthritis

Surgical options include bone grafting and fixation with K wire or screws and this could be done by open or arthroscopic methods

Complications

Nonunion

Avascular necrosis

Osteoarthritis

Avascular necrosis

The proximal fragment in scaphoid fractures may undergo avascular necrosis especially in small proximal pole fractures which are far from the scaphoid blood supply

Although revascularization and union are theoretically possible but it is unpredictable and may take many years

Avascular necrosis

small proximal pole fragments can be stabilized by a very small screw and if there is space, a bone graft from distal radius is inserted and healing is more possible if the graft is attached to an arterial pedicle or the fragment is grafted through arthroscope and stabilized with fine k wires

Avascular necrosis

If this fails, the dead fragment can be excised but the wrist tends to collapse after this procedure and arthritis develops

A better option would be a proximal row carpectomy (to remove the entire proximal row of carpal bones) or a scaphoid excision and four corner fusion (remove scaphoid and fuse the capitate, hamate, triquetrum and lunate)

Osteoarthritis

Non union or avascular necrosis may lead to secondary osteoarthritis of the wrist

If the arthritis is localized to the distal pole, excising the radial styloid may help

Osteoarthritis

As the arthritis progresses, changes appear in the scaphocapitate joint then in the capitate lunate joint; so stages of arthritis:

Stage 1 radioscaphoid arthritis

Stage 2 scaphocapitate arthritis

Stage 3 lunocapitate arthritis

The lunate radius joint is never affected, thus allowing salvage procedures either a proximal row carpectomy or four corner fusion

SNAC (Scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse)

SNAC is an end stage condition due to vascular necrosis and often requires salvage surgery in the form of a proximal row carpectomy or a wrist fusion
